candidates.title: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
candidates.author: Lance Martin, Jake Eaton, Arvin Aminpour, Emma Webb, Bharat Mediratta, Ravi Trivedi
candidates.event_date: Migration work April to September 2026 (public traffic moved to Rust in September 2026)
candidates.what_changed: Anthropic describes how it rewrote the Python Messages API (serving all Claude tokens incl. Claude Code, Cowork) in Rust using agents, and how it verified parity by turning the production API into an oracle via privacy-preserving shadow traffic, checkpoint diffs, bug fingerprints and three agent verification loops.
candidates.mechanism: Shadowing with model output replayed (model run once, output replayed to Rust, so nondeterminism and double-billing avoided). Step-by-step checkpoint comparison (accept/reject, resolve settings, build prompt; piece-by-piece within the prompt). Fingerprint record per diff (step, prompt piece, first differing byte, byte lengths of each side) with no user text. Script every 10-30 min groups records by differing fields; coordinating Claude agent alerted only on new record kinds, assigns a worker agent per kind and opens a Slack thread for humans. Inner loop: cloud sandbox with both codebases, sub-second local input check (build prompt in both, never call model) plus output check against a fake model with scripted replies; agent hypothesizes from fingerprint, writes its own request to reproduce, edits Rust until match, adds a test failing on old/passing on new. Seam: human PR review before outer loop. Outer loop: deploy, compare fingerprint frequency on builds with/without fix, stratified by logged request features (model, caching, tools, extended thinking). Memory loop: reviewer corrections saved as notes/rules (CLAUDE.md), searches for same mistake, tests, lints, and a merge check requiring matching Rust change for any Python change (or exemption).
candidates.evidence_quality: First-party, detailed, with figures (match-rate over time, CPU/memory/TTFT panels, merge counts). Numbers are self-reported; no external replication.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Partially: Katelyn Lesse (Anthropic platform eng lead) describes the same migration on The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nov 25 (same org, so not independent). Podcast says 'around five months', consistent with April to September.
candidates.relevance: High. Directly actionable pattern for agent-driven migrations: verification (not generation) as bottleneck, production as oracle, privacy-preserving diff fingerprints, layered inner/outer/memory loops, and a concrete reward-hacking example (agent copied web-search tool description into static files to make prompts match; human rejected it).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Not in prior_urls. Touches recurring themes (Edition 3 'check a record it can't edit', Edition 4 'audit the grader', Pragmatic Engineer software factories) but is new material. Outside slice B's roster (Anthropic is a lab source) so may also be picked up by the labs slice; included because the roster podcast links to it as the primary source.
candidates.summary: Messages API built in 2023 in Python ('basically a request forwarder'); by late 2025 each request is validated, converted to a prompt, tokenized and screened by safety classifiers, and output tokens are sorted into text/thinking/tool calls, with Python overhead at each step. API traffic grew roughly 1,800x from early 2024 to fall 2026. A first incremental step (Rust output parser called from Python) cut CPU only ~8-10% and each token crossed the Python/Rust boundary three times, so they went for a full rewrite. By May 2026 Claude wrote >80% of code Anthropic merged; Claude wrote a first version of the core request path in about a week. Tests were insufficient: ~700 integration tests were coupled to the Python implementation (mocks in Python memory), and an audit of ported tests found more than 100 weakened assertions; 20 binary options = >1M combinations (12 days at 1 s/test for one model). In April the Rust API passed ~98% of tests but only about a quarter of inputs matched on production traffic (e.g. Python escapes emoji in JSON tool calls, Rust wrote them raw, a few-byte prompt difference). Shadowing ran the model once and replayed output to Rust; comparison had to be exact because Claude accepts nearly any prompt so small deviations silently change replies. Diff records contain step, piece, first diff byte, and byte lengths only (no text) to protect privacy; one bug leaves the same fingerprint everywhere, and fixing an early-prompt bug can unmask others (fingerprints B and C behind A). Early on, agent fixes went through PR review and staging, taking hours or days per hypothesis; moving agents into sandboxes with sub-second local checks fixed that. Mid-May web-search example: agent proposed copying the tool description into Rust-readable files; it passed the local verifier but an engineer rejected it as throwaway, because Rust still needed to call the internal service; that service call took weeks, and memory notes let later agents link new fingerprints to the known bug instead of re-hacking. An engineer rule 'port exactly what Python did' led an agent to find seven more places the port had guessed. In June an agent grouped ~60 review comments into proposed CLAUDE.md rules, which an engineer edited and approved. Permanent checks: drift tests, lints, and a merge check requiring parallel Rust changes. Results: ~70% less CPU per request and ~20% lower median time to first token (TTFT measured on customers' Claude Code requests), no downtime or feature freeze. Lessons: verification is the new bottleneck; production system can be the verifier; design the signal (checkpoints locate, fingerprints distinguish); simple loops around strong verifiers; humans moved from inner loop to the seam (PR review in Slack) to the edge (writing rules/checks).

candidates.title: How Anthropic builds software in 2026 with Katelyn Lesse
candidates.author: Gergely Orosz (host); guest Katelyn Lesse
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-25T17:31:32Z (confirmed on page meta and post timestamp)
candidates.paywall: Free: episode, show notes and the 12 takeaways are publicly readable; transcript tab exists (not read in full). Sponsored episode.
candidates.kind: podcast / video interview with written takeaways
candidates.what_changed: Anthropic's platform engineering lead (owns Claude API and infra behind Claude Code/Desktop) describes the Python-to-Rust Messages API rewrite and how agents now handle code review routing, first-line oncall triage, onboarding, and why coding interviews were phased out.
candidates.mechanism: Rust API shadowed Python and was iterated until responses were identical; engineers looked closely at only ~20% of generated code ('As long as you can really boil something down to make it verifiable in some way, then you don't have to look at every single line'). A Claude code-review classifier runs on all PRs and decides (a) whether human review is needed at all (mechanical/low-risk e.g. SDK version bumps, model upgrades; flaky-test fixes are reviewed by another Claude which then merges and deploys), (b) how many human reviewers based on risk score plus rules, (c) which teams to route to. A Claude agent shadowed the API oncall rotation for months and now categorizes incoming alerts (real vs noise) before a human is paged; it does not yet handle incidents.
candidates.evidence_quality: Interview claims by an Anthropic leader, summarized by the host; anecdotal, no metrics beyond '~20% of code reviewed' and 'around five months'. Hard numbers are in the companion Anthropic post.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Rust migration confirmed by Anthropic's own post the same day (https://www.anthropic.com/research/migrating-api-to-rust). Code-review classifier, oncall agent, interview changes: UNVERIFIED beyond the interview.
candidates.relevance: High for practitioners: concrete, copyable patterns for risk-tiered agent code review, agent-first alert triage via shadowing an oncall rotation, agent-based interview exercises, and impact-based (not time-based) promotion criteria.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Prior issues used Pragmatic Engineer 'Software factories and code reviews' (Edition 3) and 'Inference engineering' — different episodes. New URL.
candidates.summary: 12 takeaways listed by Orosz: (1) Messages API (auth, tokenization, billing, safety checks, then GPU stack) rewritten Python->Rust in around five months by a few engineers, none Rust experts. (2) Built in Python in 2023 because the small team overlapped heavily with Research; OpenAI's API was also Python and later moved to Rust; both hit CPU footprint problems (Lesse cites a global CPU shortage). (3) A year earlier the team chose Go for new services because they could read it; by 2026 Claude was good enough at Rust; no strict code reviews, Python API used as test harness via shadowing; ~20% of code looked at closely. (4) Always-on Claude code-review classifier on every PR: no-human-review path for mechanical changes, risk-scored reviewer count, team routing. (5) Claude agent paged before humans for API oncall after months of shadowing; goal of autonomous incident handling not yet reached. (6) Onboarding is 'talk to Claude' connected to codebase/internal systems, incl. generated interactive tutorials and visualizations. (7) Planning/alignment time unchanged from pre-AI; average engineer spends more time coordinating than implementing. (8) Still two-pizza teams of ~5-8 that own systems and oncall. (9) Engineers build much more internal tooling, e.g. a Slack channel running a multi-agent team toward one goal. (10) Knowing a language well matters less. (11) Coding interview phased out after strong candidates kept failing it (they no longer hand-write code); experimenting with interviews done together with coding agents; design and project deep-dive interviews unchanged. (12) For promotions, time-to-complete is meaningless; evaluated by impact (CPU saved, latency reduced, incidents avoided). Also mentions a PM shipping a feature to production, Anthropic's 'software factory', building Claude Managed Agents. Host notes Anthropic became public last week at ~$1T market cap (UNVERIFIED here; host claim). Programming note: no The Pulse on Nov 26 (Thanksgiving).
